decks.title: Water of Crystallisation — Part 1: Hydrates, anhydrous salts, heating hydrates and percentage of water
goals: Define water of crystallisation and write the formulae of the prescribed hydrated salts
Name anhydrous salts and describe what happens when a hydrate is heated
Calculate the percentage of water of crystallisation in a hydrated salt

slides.heading: Water of Crystallisation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — water locked inside crystals, and what happens when it is driven out.

visual.alt: Flow: blue crystals are heated and give a white powder and water vapour

slides.narration: Blue crystals of copper sulphate look completely dry. Yet heat them gently and drops of water appear, while the crystals crumble to a white powder. The water was inside the crystals all along.

slides.heading: Hydrated salts
slides.body_md: **Water of crystallisation** is the fixed number of water molecules that combine chemically with one formula unit of a salt when it crystallises from solution. A salt that has it is **hydrated**.

visual.alt: Table of four hydrated salts with formulae and colours

slides.narration: Each hydrate holds a fixed number of water molecules for every unit of the salt. Copper sulphate holds five, ferrous sulphate seven, and washing soda and Glauber salt ten each. The water is part of the crystal, not wet on the surface.

slides.heading: Anhydrous substances
slides.body_md: **Anhydrous** means "without water". An anhydrous salt has **no water of crystallisation**, however it was dried.

visual.alt: Table of four anhydrous salts with formulae

slides.narration: Some salts crystallise with no water at all. Sodium nitrate, potassium chloride, lead chloride and potassium sulphate are examples. Their crystals do not give water drops on heating.

slides.heading: Quick check: hydrate or not
slides.body_md: Which of these salts has water of crystallisation?
slides.narration: Look for the dot followed by a number of water molecules.

slides.heading: Heating a hydrate
slides.body_md: Use a **hard glass** tube with its mouth **slightly downwards**, so that water formed does not run back onto the hot glass.

visual.alt: A test tube of hydrated crystals heated in a clamp, with drops of water collecting near the mouth

slides.narration: Put a little of the crystals in a dry hard glass test tube. Clamp it with the mouth slightly downwards and heat gently. Water vapour leaves the crystals and condenses as drops on the cooler part of the tube. Tilting the mouth down stops the water running back and cracking the hot glass.

slides.heading: What you see on heating

visual.alt: Table of observations on heating four hydrates

slides.narration: All four hydrates crumble to a powder on heating, and drops of water collect in the cooler part of the tube. Blue copper sulphate and pale green ferrous sulphate also lose their colour, because the colour belongs to the hydrated form.

slides.heading: Quick check: the observation
slides.body_md: When blue crystals of hydrated copper sulphate are gently heated in a dry test tube, the residue is…
slides.narration: Think about what colour the crystals lose.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: heating ferrous sulphate crystals
slides.body_md: A student heats pale green crystals of ferrous sulphate in a dry test tube. Write the balanced equation and state two observations.
bullets: Step 1: the crystals lose all seven molecules of water of crystallisation.
Step 2: equation: $\ce{FeSO4.7H2O ->[\Delta] FeSO4 + 7H2O}$.
Step 3: observations: the pale green crystals crumble to a whitish powder, and drops of water collect on the cooler part of the tube.

visual.alt: Equation: ferrous sulphate heptahydrate on heating gives anhydrous ferrous sulphate and seven molecules of water
visual.caption: Heating ferrous sulphate crystals

slides.narration: Write the hydrate on the left and the anhydrous salt and the water on the right. All seven water molecules leave, so the equation balances with seven waters. You would see pale green crystals crumbling to a whitish powder, with drops of water in the tube.

slides.heading: A test for water
slides.body_md: White **anhydrous copper sulphate** turns **blue** when water is added, and gets hot. The change can be reversed by heating.

visual.alt: Reversible change between blue hydrated copper sulphate and white anhydrous copper sulphate
visual.caption: Reversible change

slides.narration: White anhydrous copper sulphate takes up water and turns blue again, giving out a little heat. Heating the blue crystals turns them white. This reversible change makes a handy test for the presence of water.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: percentage of water in a hydrate
slides.body_md: Calculate the percentage of water of crystallisation in FeSO₄·7H₂O. (Fe = 56, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1)
bullets: Step 1: relative molecular mass of FeSO₄ = 56 + 32 + 4 × 16 = 152.
Step 2: seven water molecules = 7 × 18 = 126; the hydrate = 152 + 126 = 278.
Step 3: percentage of water = 126 ÷ 278 × 100 = **45.3%**.

visual.alt: Worked table: ferrous sulphate one hundred and fifty-two, water one hundred and twenty-six, hydrate two hundred and seventy-eight, water forty-five point three per cent

slides.narration: Find the mass of the anhydrous salt, then the mass of the water, and add them to get the hydrate. Water is one hundred and twenty six out of two hundred and seventy eight. Divide and multiply by one hundred to get about forty-five per cent.

slides.heading: Percentage of water in four hydrates

visual.alt: Table of the relative mass of each hydrate, the mass of its water and the percentage of water

slides.narration: Compare the four. Washing soda is nearly two thirds water by mass, while copper sulphate is only about a third. The more water molecules per formula unit, the greater the share, but the mass of the salt matters too.

slides.heading: Quick check: a percentage
slides.body_md: Atomic masses: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16, H = 1. The percentage of water in Na₂CO₃·10H₂O is…
slides.narration: Ten waters out of the whole hydrate. Divide the mass of the water by the mass of the hydrate.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: mass of residue
slides.body_md: Heating 5.56 g of FeSO₄·7H₂O drives off all the water. Find the mass of anhydrous FeSO₄ left.
bullets: Step 1: 278 g of hydrate gives 152 g of FeSO₄.
Step 3: check: water lost = 5.56 − 3.04 = 2.52 g.

visual.alt: Worked table: five point five six grams of hydrate leaves three point zero four grams of residue and loses two point five two grams of water

slides.narration: Use the ratio of the masses. The anhydrous salt is one hundred and fifty two parts in every two hundred and seventy eight parts of hydrate. Scale that to your sample to get the residue, and subtract from the starting mass to check the water lost.

slides.heading: Quick check: anhydrous crystals
slides.body_md: True or false: crystals of anhydrous potassium chloride contain water of crystallisation.
slides.narration: What does anhydrous mean?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Water of crystallisation: fixed water molecules combined with a salt in its crystals.
Hydrates: CuSO₄·5H₂O, FeSO₄·7H₂O, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, Na₂SO₄·10H₂O. Anhydrous: NaNO₃, KCl, PbCl₂, K₂SO₄.
Heating a hydrate: powder, loss of colour in coloured hydrates, drops of water.
Percentage of water = mass of water ÷ mass of hydrate × 100.

visual.alt: Summary table of colour changes on heating hydrates

slides.narration: To recap. Hydrated salts hold a fixed number of water molecules inside their crystals. Heating drives the water off, leaving an anhydrous powder and drops of water in the tube. The share of water comes from the relative molecular masses.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **dot** and the **number** in a hydrate formula, and balance the water in the equation.
Name the **colour change** and mention **drops of water** in a heating observation.
Show **each mass** in a percentage calculation and state the atomic masses used.
Do not call a dried salt anhydrous unless it never had water of crystallisation or all of it has been removed.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write the dot and the number in a hydrate formula and balance the water. Describe the colour change and the drops of water when heating. Show every mass in a percentage calculation. And use the word anhydrous with care.

decks.title: Water of Crystallisation — Part 2: Efflorescence, deliquescence, hygroscopy, drying and dehydrating agents
goals: Distinguish efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic substances with examples
Distinguish a drying agent from a dehydrating agent using quicklime and concentrated sulphuric acid
Choose a suitable drying agent for a gas

slides.heading: Left in the Open Air
slides.body_md: Part 2 — substances that lose or gain water when exposed to air, and the agents that remove water.

visual.alt: Flow: in the open air a substance may lose water or gain water

slides.narration: Leave a jar of washing soda crystals open and they crumble. Leave ferric chloride open and it turns into a puddle. Leave concentrated sulphuric acid open and it grows. Air carries water vapour, and different substances treat it differently.

slides.heading: Efflorescence, deliquescence, hygroscopy
slides.body_md: All three depend on **moisture in the air**.

rows: A hydrate loses its water of crystallisation to dry air and crumbles to powder
A solid absorbs moisture from the air and dissolves in it to form a solution
Ferric chloride, sodium hydroxide, anhydrous calcium chloride
A substance absorbs moisture from the air, usually without dissolving

visual.alt: Table defining efflorescence, deliquescence and hygroscopy with examples

slides.narration: Efflorescence is loss of water of crystallisation. Deliquescence is taking in so much moisture that the solid dissolves. Hygroscopy is taking in moisture from the air without becoming a solution. Notice that the first loses water while the others gain it.

slides.heading: Three dishes in the open air
slides.body_md: Efflorescence **loses** water; deliquescence and hygroscopy **gain** water.

slides.heading: Quick check: crumbling crystals
slides.body_md: Colourless crystals left in an open dish crumble to a white powder with no gain in mass. The change is…
slides.narration: Is water lost or gained?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: efflorescence of washing soda
slides.body_md: 2.86 g of washing soda crystals lose nine of their ten molecules of water on standing in dry air. (Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16, H = 1.) Find the mass of the powder left.
bullets: Step 1: equation: $\ce{Na2CO3.10H2O -> Na2CO3.H2O + 9H2O}$.
Step 2: Mr of the crystals = 286; Mr of the powder = 106 + 18 = 124.

visual.alt: Equation: washing soda loses nine molecules of water to give the monohydrate
visual.caption: Efflorescence of washing soda

slides.narration: Write the equation first. The crystals keep one molecule of water and lose nine. The powder is one hundred and twenty four parts out of every two hundred and eighty six parts of crystals, so scale that to your sample to find the mass of the powder.

slides.heading: Quick check: a puddle
slides.body_md: A solid left in the open air gains mass and finally forms a solution. This behaviour is called…
slides.narration: It takes in water until it dissolves in it.

slides.heading: Telling them apart
slides.body_md: Ask two questions: does the **mass rise or fall**, and does the substance **dissolve**?

nodes.label: Mass falls: loses water of crystallisation

visual.alt: Flow chart separating efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic substances by change in mass and whether the substance dissolves

slides.narration: Use the flow chart. If the mass falls and the crystals crumble, the substance is efflorescent. If the mass rises and a solution forms, it is deliquescent. If the mass rises with no solution, it is hygroscopic.

slides.heading: Drying agent or dehydrating agent?
slides.body_md: A **drying agent** takes up water or water vapour from a substance **without reacting with it**. A **dehydrating agent** removes **water chemically combined** in a compound, or even the elements of water (hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio two to one).

rows: Moisture mixed with a gas or a liquid
Combined water, or H and O in the ratio 2 to 1
Quicklime (for ammonia), concentrated sulphuric acid (for hydrogen)

visual.alt: Table comparing drying agents and dehydrating agents

slides.narration: A drying agent only takes away moisture, leaving the dried substance unchanged. A dehydrating agent pulls out water that is part of a compound, so a new substance is formed. Concentrated sulphuric acid can do both, but quicklime is only a drying agent.

slides.heading: Drying a gas
slides.body_md: Match the agent to the gas: a **neutral or acidic** gas through **concentrated sulphuric acid**; **ammonia** through **quicklime**.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: choose the drying agent
slides.body_md: Moist hydrogen and moist ammonia are each to be dried. Choose an agent for each and give a reason.

Step 2: ammonia reacts with the acid: $\ce{2NH3 + H2SO4 -> (NH4)2SO4}$, so the acid is unsuitable.
Step 3: ammonia does not react with quicklime, so it is dried over lumps of quicklime.

slides.narration: A drying agent must not react with the gas it dries. Hydrogen does not react with the acid, so the acid is fine. Ammonia, a base, reacts with the acid to make a salt, so quicklime is used for it.

slides.heading: Concentrated sulphuric acid as a dehydrating agent
slides.body_md: It removes **combined water**: blue crystals of copper sulphate turn **white**, and sugar is **charred to black carbon**.

visual.alt: Equation: concentrated sulphuric acid removes the elements of water from sugar and leaves carbon
visual.caption: Dehydration of sugar

slides.narration: The acid pulls out the water that is built into a compound. Blue crystals lose their water of crystallisation and turn white. Sugar loses hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio of water and is left as black carbon. This is dehydration, not mere drying.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Efflorescent: loses water of crystallisation (washing soda). Deliquescent: absorbs moisture and dissolves (ferric chloride). Hygroscopic: absorbs moisture (quicklime, concentrated sulphuric acid).
Drying agent: removes moisture, no reaction. Dehydrating agent: removes combined water.
Dry ammonia with quicklime; dry hydrogen with concentrated sulphuric acid.

slides.narration: To recap. Efflorescent substances lose water, deliquescent ones dissolve in water from the air, and hygroscopic ones take it in. A drying agent removes moisture without a reaction, while a dehydrating agent removes combined water.

bullets: Efflorescence is a **loss** of water; the other two are **gains**.
Give a **named example** with each definition.
For drying gases, say why the agent does **not react** with the gas.
Quote the **observation** for dehydration: blue to white, or sugar to black.

sections.heading: 1. Water of crystallisation; hydrated and anhydrous substances
sections.body_md:
**Water of crystallisation** is the fixed number of water molecules that combine chemically with one formula unit of a salt when it crystallises from solution. Such a salt is **hydrated**; a salt without it is **anhydrous**.

| Hydrated salt | Formula | Colour of crystals | Colour of anhydrous form |
|---|---|---|---|
| Copper sulphate pentahydrate (blue vitriol) | CuSO₄·5H₂O | Blue | White |
| Ferrous sulphate heptahydrate (green vitriol) | FeSO₄·7H₂O | Pale green | Whitish |
| Sodium carbonate decahydrate (washing soda) | Na₂CO₃·10H₂O | Colourless | White |
| Sodium sulphate decahydrate (Glauber's salt) | Na₂SO₄·10H₂O | Colourless | White |

**Anhydrous salts** (no water of crystallisation): sodium nitrate NaNO₃, potassium chloride KCl, lead chloride PbCl₂, potassium sulphate K₂SO₄.

**Heating a hydrate** (dry hard glass test tube, mouth slightly downwards): the crystals crumble to a powder, coloured hydrates lose their colour and drops of water collect on the cooler part of the tube.

**A test for water:** white anhydrous copper sulphate turns blue on adding water (heat is given out); heating the blue crystals turns them white again.

**Percentage of water of crystallisation** = (mass of water in one formula unit ÷ relative molecular mass of the hydrate) × 100. With H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23, S = 32, Fe = 56, Cu = 63.5, C = 12:

| Hydrate | Mass of hydrate | Mass of water | Per cent water |
|---|---|---|---|
| CuSO₄·5H₂O | 249.5 | 90 | 36.1 |
| FeSO₄·7H₂O | 278 | 126 | 45.3 |
| Na₂SO₄·10H₂O | 322 | 180 | 55.9 |
| Na₂CO₃·10H₂O | 286 | 180 | 62.9 |

Ferrous sulphate crystals are described as pale green and the residue as whitish; books vary slightly.

A salt whose crystals contain water of crystallisation.

sections.heading: 2. Efflorescence, deliquescence and hygroscopy
sections.body_md:
| Term | What happens | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Efflorescence** | A hydrate loses its water of crystallisation (wholly or partly) to dry air at ordinary temperature and crumbles to powder | Washing soda, Glauber's salt |
| **Deliquescence** | A solid takes moisture from the air and dissolves in it to form a solution | Ferric chloride, sodium hydroxide, anhydrous calcium chloride |
| **Hygroscopy** | A substance absorbs moisture from the air, usually without dissolving | Quicklime, concentrated sulphuric acid |

- Efflorescence **loses** water; deliquescence and hygroscopy **gain** it. Washing soda changes to the monohydrate, Na₂CO₃·H₂O, when it effloresces.
- A **deliquescent** substance is also hygroscopic; a hygroscopic substance need not be deliquescent. Books group some substances (for example anhydrous calcium chloride) differently; the examples above are the usual ICSE ones.
- Efflorescent crystals **lose mass**; deliquescent and hygroscopic substances **gain mass**.
- **Example:** 28.6 g of washing soda crystals that fully change to the monohydrate leave 12.4 g of powder (16.2 g of water lost).

key_terms.definition_md: Loss of water of crystallisation by a hydrate on exposure to dry air.
Absorption of moisture from air by a solid so that it dissolves to form a solution.
A substance that absorbs moisture from the air.

sections.heading: 3. Drying agents and dehydrating agents
sections.body_md:
| | Drying agent | Dehydrating agent |
|---|---|---|
| Removes | Moisture mixed with a gas or liquid | Water that is chemically combined, or the elements hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2 : 1 |
| Substance dried | Not changed | A new substance is formed |
| Examples | Quicklime (CaO), concentrated sulphuric acid | Concentrated sulphuric acid |

**Drying gases:** a drying agent must **not react** with the gas.
- Concentrated sulphuric acid (in a wash bottle) dries hydrogen, chlorine and hydrogen chloride, but **not ammonia**, which reacts with it: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄.
- **Quicklime** (lumps in a drying tower) dries **ammonia**.

**Dehydrating action of concentrated sulphuric acid:** blue crystals of copper sulphate turn **white** (the combined water is removed); sugar is **charred to black carbon**: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ → 12C + 11H₂O (hydrogen and oxygen leave in the ratio of water). Quicklime is a **drying agent**, not a dehydrating agent.

key_terms.definition_md: A substance that removes moisture from a gas or liquid without reacting with it.
A substance that removes water, or the elements of water, that is chemically combined in a compound.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing a hydrate formula without the **dot** and the **number**, or leaving the water out of the equation.
- Forgetting the **colour change** and the **drops of water** when a hydrate is heated.
- Mixing up efflorescence (a **loss** of water) with deliquescence (a **gain** that ends in a solution).
- Drying ammonia with concentrated sulphuric acid: it **reacts** with the gas.
- Calling quicklime a dehydrating agent; it is a **drying agent**.
- In a percentage calculation, forgetting to include all the water molecules in the mass of the hydrate.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a formula, a colour change, an observation or a term.
- 2 marks: a balanced equation or two differences, matched point for point.
- 3 marks: a short calculation with working, or a drying agent chosen with a reason.
- 10-mark structured question: a situation or diagram followed by parts such as equations, observations, a calculation and a labelled diagram.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between efflorescence and deliquescence, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Efflorescence:** a hydrate **loses** water of crystallisation to dry air and crumbles to powder (washing soda). **Deliquescence:** a solid **absorbs moisture** from the air and **dissolves** in it (ferric chloride).

questions.solution_md: Loses water, powder; absorbs water, solution; with examples.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a drying agent and a dehydrating agent, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: A **drying agent** removes moisture **without reacting** with the substance dried (**quicklime** for ammonia). A **dehydrating agent** removes **combined water** or the elements of water from a compound (**concentrated sulphuric acid** with sugar).

questions.solution_md: Moisture only; combined water; examples.

A jar holds 28.6 g of colourless washing soda crystals, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O. It is left unstoppered in dry weather until the crystals have changed completely to white powder, Na₂CO₃·H₂O. (Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16, H = 1)

(a) Name this behaviour. [1]

(b) Write a balanced equation for the change. [2]

(c) Calculate the mass of powder left. [3]

(d) Calculate the percentage of the original mass that is lost. [2]

(e) Name one substance that is deliquescent and state how its mass would change in damp air. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Efflorescence.**

**(b)** $\ce{Na2CO3.10H2O -> Na2CO3.H2O + 9H2O}$

**(c)** Mr of crystals = 286; powder = 124. Mass left = 28.6 × 124 ÷ 286 = **12.4 g**.

**(d)** Lost = 28.6 − 12.4 = 16.2 g; 16.2 ÷ 28.6 × 100 = **56.6%**.

**(e)** **Ferric chloride** (or sodium hydroxide); its mass **increases** as it absorbs moisture and dissolves.

questions.solution_md: Efflorescence; equation; 12.4 g; 56.6%; ferric chloride gains mass.

questions.stem_md:
Three substances are left in the open air. Dish X holds washing soda crystals, dish Y holds 5 g of solid ferric chloride and beaker Z holds 100 g of concentrated sulphuric acid.

(a) Name the behaviour of X, Y and Z. [3]

(b) Which one loses mass? [1]

(c) The ferric chloride becomes a liquid weighing 8 g. Calculate the mass of water absorbed and the percentage increase in mass. [2]

(d) The acid is weighed again and weighs 109 g. Calculate the percentage gain in its mass. [2]

(e) Explain why a bottle of concentrated sulphuric acid should be kept closed. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** X: **efflorescent**; Y: **deliquescent**; Z: **hygroscopic**.

**(b)** **X**.

**(c)** Water absorbed = 8 − 5 = **3 g**; increase = 3 ÷ 5 × 100 = **60%**.

**(d)** Gain = 109 − 100 = 9 g; 9 ÷ 100 × 100 = **9%**.

**(e)** The acid **absorbs water vapour from the air** and becomes **dilute**, so it loses its drying and dehydrating power.

questions.solution_md: Efflorescent, deliquescent, hygroscopic; X; 3 g and 60%; 9%; the acid absorbs vapour.

questions.stem_md:
A few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid are added to a spoonful of sugar in a beaker, and a second dry beaker contains lumps of quicklime.

(a) State two observations in the beaker with sugar. [2]

(b) Write the equation for the change that takes place in sugar. [2]

(c) Name the property of the acid that is shown. [1]

(d) State the observation when blue copper sulphate crystals are placed in the acid. [2]

(e) Explain why quicklime is a drying agent but not a dehydrating agent. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The sugar **turns black** (and a hot, steaming mass swells).

**(b)** $\ce{C12H22O11 ->[\text{conc. H2SO4}] 12C + 11H2O}$

**(c)** **Dehydrating** action (removal of the elements of water).

**(d)** The **blue crystals turn white**.

**(e)** Quicklime only **absorbs moisture** from gases or liquids without reacting with them; it **does not remove combined water** or the elements of water from compounds like sugar.

questions.solution_md: Sugar black; equation; dehydrating; blue to white; quicklime only absorbs moisture.

questions.stem_md:
A student heats 16.1 g of Glauber's salt, Na₂SO₄·10H₂O, until the mass is constant. (Na = 23, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1)

(a) Calculate the relative molecular mass of the hydrate. [2]

(b) Calculate the percentage of water of crystallisation. [2]

(c) Calculate the mass of anhydrous sodium sulphate left. [3]

(d) Write the balanced equation for the heating. [1]

(e) State one observation in the test tube during the heating. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Na₂SO₄ = 142; 10H₂O = 180; hydrate = **322**.

**(b)** 180 ÷ 322 × 100 = **55.9%**.

**(c)** Residue = 16.1 × 142 ÷ 322 = **7.1 g**.

**(d)** $\ce{Na2SO4.10H2O ->[\Delta] Na2SO4 + 10H2O}$

**(e)** The **colourless crystals crumble to a white powder** and **drops of water** collect on the cooler part of the tube.

questions.solution_md: 322; 55.9%; 7.1 g; equation; powder and drops of water.
